910.name: Illyrian and Roman Bosnia
910.description: Illyrian tribal settlement in the Bosnian highlands, Roman conquest and provincial administration, military colony development, and the spread of Christianity through the Dalmatian hinterland.

sub_clusters.name: Illyrian Tribes of Bosnia
sub_clusters.description: The Daesitiates, Autariatae, and other Illyrian tribes inhabiting the mountainous interior of Bosnia, their hillforts, and resistance to Roman expansion.

sub_clusters.name: Roman Provincial Rule
sub_clusters.description: Bosnia as part of the Roman provinces of Dalmatia and Pannonia, the Bato rebellion, mining operations, and the strategic importance of the region in the Roman frontier system.

920.name: Medieval Bosnian Kingdom
920.description: The emergence of a distinct Bosnian polity from Slavic settlement through the medieval Bosnian Banate and Kingdom, including the distinctive Bosnian Church and the Bogomil heresy.

sub_clusters.name: Slavic Settlement and Early Banate
sub_clusters.description: South Slavic settlement of Bosnia, the emergence of the Banate of Bosnia, and the region's position between Hungarian, Byzantine, and Serbian spheres of influence.

sub_clusters.name: Ban Kulin and the Bosnian Golden Age
sub_clusters.description: The reign of Ban Kulin (1180–1204) as a period of prosperity and relative independence, his famous charter, and the early appearance of the Bosnian Church.
key_events: Ban Kulin's Charter — earliest Bosnian state document (1189)
Ban Kulin's abjuration of heresy under papal pressure (1203)

sub_clusters.name: Bogomil Heresy and the Bosnian Church
sub_clusters.description: The distinctive Bosnian Church (Crkva bosanska), its disputed connection to Bogomilism, papal crusades against Bosnian heretics, and the stećci tombstone tradition.

sub_clusters.name: Bosnian Kingdom and Tvrtko I
sub_clusters.description: The expansion of Bosnia under the Kotromanić dynasty, the coronation of Tvrtko I as King (1377), Bosnia's territorial peak, and the subsequent decline leading to Ottoman conquest.

930.name: Ottoman Conquest and Early Ottoman Bosnia
930.description: The Ottoman conquest of Bosnia in 1463, mass conversion to Islam, the development of a distinctive Bosnian Muslim (Bosniak) identity, and the flourishing of Ottoman urban culture in Sarajevo and Mostar.

sub_clusters.name: Ottoman Conquest (1463)
sub_clusters.description: Sultan Mehmed II's rapid conquest of the Bosnian Kingdom, the execution of the last king Stefan Tomašević, and the fall of Herzegovina to the Ottomans.
key_events: Ottoman conquest of Bosnia; last Bosnian King Stefan Tomašević executed (1463)

sub_clusters.name: Islamization and Ottoman Urban Culture
sub_clusters.description: The gradual conversion of Bosnian nobility and peasants to Islam, the construction of mosques, bridges (Stari Most), and bazaars, and the development of Sarajevo as a major Ottoman provincial center.

940.name: Ottoman Decline and Austro-Hungarian Annexation
940.description: The decline of Ottoman authority in Bosnia, the Bosnian uprising of 1831, Austro-Hungarian occupation and annexation, and the rise of South Slav nationalism culminating in the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand.

sub_clusters.name: Late Ottoman Bosnia and Revolts
sub_clusters.description: The decline of Ottoman control, the Husein Gradaščević revolt (1831), peasant uprisings of 1875, and the Great Eastern Crisis that led to Austro-Hungarian intervention.

sub_clusters.name: Austro-Hungarian Rule (1878–1914)
sub_clusters.description: The Congress of Berlin's grant of occupation rights to Austria-Hungary, the formal annexation of 1908 (Bosnian Crisis), modernization of infrastructure, and growing ethnic-national tensions.

sub_clusters.name: Sarajevo Assassination (1914)
sub_clusters.description: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie by Gavrilo Princip in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, the event that triggered the chain of alliances leading to World War I.
key_events: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo triggers World War I (June 28, 1914)

950.name: World Wars and Yugoslav Era
950.description: Bosnia's experience in both World Wars, the complex multi-faction fighting of WWII, and the country's position as a constituent republic within Tito's socialist Yugoslavia.

sub_clusters.name: WWI and Interwar Yugoslavia
sub_clusters.description: Bosnia's incorporation into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (1918), the uncertain national status of Bosniaks, and interwar political tensions between Serb and Croat visions.

sub_clusters.name: WWII Multi-Faction Warfare
sub_clusters.description: Bosnia as the epicenter of WWII Yugoslav fighting: the Ustasha NDH regime, Chetnik Serbian royalists, Tito's Partisans, and the devastation inflicted on all communities, especially Serbs, Jews, and Roma.

sub_clusters.name: Titoist Yugoslavia and Bosnian Identity
sub_clusters.description: Bosnia's role within socialist Yugoslavia, the 1984 Sarajevo Winter Olympics, the recognition of 'Muslim' as a national category (1971), and the rise of nationalism after Tito's death.

960.name: Bosnian War and Dayton Peace
960.description: The devastating Bosnian War (1992–1995), the Siege of Sarajevo, the Srebrenica genocide, and the Dayton Agreement that ended the conflict and established the current political framework.

sub_clusters.name: Siege of Sarajevo
sub_clusters.description: The longest siege of a capital city in modern warfare (1,425 days), Serb forces' bombardment, the Sarajevo tunnel, sniper alley, and the international community's failure to intervene effectively.
key_events: Siege of Sarajevo begins — longest siege in modern warfare (April 1992–February 1996)

sub_clusters.name: Srebrenica Genocide
sub_clusters.description: The massacre of over 8,000 Bosniak men and boys by Bosnian Serb forces in the UN-designated safe area of Srebrenica in July 1995, the worst atrocity in Europe since WWII.
key_events: Srebrenica genocide — over 8,000 Bosniaks killed in UN safe area (July 1995)

sub_clusters.name: Dayton Agreement (1995)
sub_clusters.description: The General Framework Agreement for Peace signed in Dayton, Ohio, creating the complex dual-entity structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the Federation and Republika Srpska.

960.name: Post-War Governance and EU Path
960.description: Bosnia's complex post-Dayton political system, the Office of the High Representative, ICTY war crimes proceedings, ethnic political deadlock, and the slow path toward EU integration.

sub_clusters.name: High Representative and State-Building
sub_clusters.description: The Office of the High Representative's Bonn Powers, imposition of laws and removal of officials, ICTY prosecutions including Karadžić and Mladić, and international peacekeeping operations.

sub_clusters.name: Ethnic Deadlock and EU Candidacy
sub_clusters.description: Continued constitutional deadlock between the three constituent peoples, the Sejdić-Finci ruling on minority rights, EU candidate status (2022), and ongoing reform challenges.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
